title: Measuring a creek
teaches: An orange, a stopwatch and a USGS gauge page: discharge measured by hand
summary: **Discharge is volume per second.** It is the average speed of the water times the area of the cross-section.
**An orange times the surface speed.** It floats low, so it moves with the water and the wind barely pushes it.
**The surface is the fastest water.** The bed holds back the water near it, and the average over the depth is about 0.8 of the surface speed.
**Measure the cross-section in pieces.** Width with a tape and depths at even steps; adding up panels, each with its own speed, gives a better total than one average.
**The deep middle carries most of the water.** It is both deeper and faster, so at low flow a third of the width can carry two thirds of the water.
**A gauge measures stage, not discharge.** Stage is the height of the water above the gauge's own zero, read every fifteen minutes.
**A rating curve turns stage into discharge.** It is drawn through measurements made by hand, bends upward, and shifts when a flood moves the gravel below the gauge.
**Big rivers peak late.** A city creek peaks within hours of the heaviest rain; a big river many hours after it, as water from the far parts of its basin arrives.

blocks.text: Piper's Creek runs down a wooded ravine in Carkeek Park, in north Seattle, to the Sound. On a summer afternoon it is a few strides wide and ankle deep in most places, clear over gravel. How much water goes past, in litres every second? That number is the creek's **discharge**, from lesson 2: the volume of water crossing a line across the stream each second.

A **gauge** is a station on a river that records its level through the day. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) runs gauges on many Washington rivers and works out from each level a discharge every fifteen minutes. You can measure a creek's discharge yourself with an orange, a stopwatch, a tape measure and a metre stick, and get close enough to be useful. This lesson does that, then reads a USGS gauge page to see how the same job is done on the Cedar River at Renton and the Snoqualmie near Carnation.

blocks.caption: Three Seattle creeks that suit a measurement, and the USGS gauge on the Cedar River near its mouth.

blocks.text: Speed first. Find a straight stretch where the water runs smoothly, without eddies or snags, and mark 10 m along the bank with two sticks. Drop an orange in the water a few metres above the first stick, so it is moving at the creek's speed when it passes. Start the stopwatch as it passes the first stick and stop it at the second. Do it three times and take the average. If the orange takes 25 s to go 10 m, the surface water is moving at 0.4 m/s.

An orange suits the job because it floats low, with only a cap of peel showing above the water. The rest rides in the current, so it moves with the water and the wind barely pushes it, and it is bright enough to follow. A leaf or a stick sits on top and catches the breeze. Fish the orange out at the end.

The orange measures the surface, and the surface carries the fastest water in the creek. The bed holds back the water touching it, that water slows the layer above, and so on upward, so the speed grows from near zero at the bed to its greatest at the top. Over a gravel bed the average over the whole depth comes out at about 0.8 of the surface speed, a little more over smooth sand and a little less over boulders. The same shape puts that average speed about six-tenths of the way down, which is where hydrographers hold their meters.[^sixtenths] So 0.4 m/s at the surface means about 0.32 m/s on average.

blocks.caption: The speed of the water at each depth over a rough bed, in a model: the arrows are speeds, longest at the surface where the orange floats. The dashed line is the average over the depth, about 0.8 of the surface speed, which the water about six-tenths of the way down has.

blocks.text: Now the size of the stream. Halfway along your 10 m, stretch the tape across from water's edge to water's edge and measure the depth with a metre stick at even steps, every half metre in a small creek, starting a quarter metre in from the edge so each reading stands in the middle of its own half-metre strip. Suppose the creek is 3.0 m wide and the depths at the six points are 6, 16, 30, 34, 20 and 8 cm. Their average, 19 cm, times the width gives the area of the cross-section, 0.57 m².

The quick estimate is then average speed times area: 0.32 m/s × 0.57 m² ≈ 0.18 m³/s. That is 180 litres a second, or about 6.4 cubic feet a second (cfs), the unit on American gauge pages.[^cfs] A bathtub holds something like 150 to 200 litres, so about a bathtub's worth goes past every second.

That gives the whole creek the speed of the deepest lane, where the orange ran, and the creek doesn't move that way. The shallow water at the edges, with the bed close beneath it, is slower. Hydrographers, the people who measure rivers for a living, split the stream into **panels**, a strip of width around each measuring point, and multiply each panel's own area by its own speed.[^midsection] The figure does that, starting from the six depths above, which you can change. Since only the orange's lane is timed, it takes the speed at each point to grow with that point's depth, a rule that holds roughly in real streams.

blocks.caption: A model creek 3 m wide, measured at six points half a metre apart. Each panel's shading and number give its share of the discharge; the speed at each point grows with its depth.
blocks.task: Guess the middle third's share, then set the creek after a storm: the water 20 cm higher and the orange taking 8 s

blocks.text: Two things come out of it. At this low summer flow the middle third of the width carries about two thirds of the water, since it is both the deepest and the fastest part, so a depth misread in the middle matters far more than one misread at the edge. When the water rises, the edges deepen too and their share grows. And the panel sum, 0.14 m³/s, is about a fifth lower than the quick estimate, because the panels give the shallow edges their own slower speeds. Six points are enough to show the method. A USGS hydrographer measures at twenty or more points with a current meter, and a good measurement is within about five percent of the true flow.

Raise the water by 20 cm and let the orange cover the 10 m in 8 s, as after a winter storm, and the discharge grows nearly sevenfold. Deeper water moves faster, and there is more of it moving. That pairing is why a gauge needs only the height of the water to know its discharge, as the next part shows.

**Measure your own.** In late summer, when the creeks are lowest and clearest, take an orange, a stopwatch, a tape and a metre stick to Piper's Creek, Thornton Creek or Longfellow Creek and work out the discharge. Use the park's car park and its trails down to the water rather than scrambling down a ravine bank. Wade only where the water is below your knees and too slow to push at your legs. After heavy rain a city creek can rise past that within minutes, so on a wet day stay on the bank. Keep off the gravel in autumn and winter, when salmon returning to several of Seattle's creeks may have laid eggs in it, and wash your hands afterwards, since city creeks carry what washes off the streets. After a big November rain, come back and time an orange from the bank alone: with the summer depths you cannot use, the speed by itself shows how much faster the creek is running.

The USGS gauge on the Cedar River at Renton, station 12119000, stands near the river's mouth at Lake Washington, downstream of Seattle's Masonry Dam. Like most USGS gauges it does not measure discharge directly. It measures **stage**: the height of the water surface above a fixed zero of the gauge's own, which is not the depth of the river. Every fifteen minutes it reads the stage, with a float in a stilling well,[^well] a pressure sensor in the water or a radar looking down from a bridge, and sends the readings out by satellite.

To see them, go to USGS Water Data, waterdata.usgs.gov, and search for the station number, 12119000 for the Cedar at Renton or 12149000 for the Snoqualmie near Carnation. The page shows two lines: **gage height** in feet, and discharge in cubic feet per second. The USGS spells the word gage, an older American spelling the agency has kept in its official names; it is the same thing as a gauge.

The discharge on that page comes from the stage through a **rating curve**. Every month or two, and during floods when they can, hydrographers go to the gauge and measure the discharge the long way: wading across with a current meter, point by point as you did with the metre stick, or crossing from a bridge or a boat with an acoustic instrument that reads the speed of the water at every depth. Each visit gives one point, a stage and a discharge measured together. Over the years the points trace a curve, and every fifteen minutes the new stage is looked up on the curve to give that moment's discharge.

blocks.caption: A model rating curve for a large river: the channel at the gauge above, and below it the discharge for each stage, with the curve drawn through the hydrographers' measurements. The switch shows the gauge after a flood has piled gravel on the bar below it.
blocks.task: Guess how the discharge changes from 4 ft to 8 ft, then take the river to 8 ft and switch on the flood's gravel

blocks.text: The curve bends upward for the reason the creek showed: as the water rises it gets wider and deeper and faster, so each foot of stage adds more flow than the foot before. On this model gauge the water stops flowing at a stage of 2 ft, so a rise from 4 ft to 8 ft triples the depth of water flowing over the bar, from 2 ft to 6 ft, and the discharge grows about eight times.

A rating curve is only as good as the channel is steady. The stage at a gauge is set by its **control**: whatever just downstream holds the water back, such as a gravel bar, a rock ledge or a narrowing. A flood can scour the bar away or pile more gravel on it. A higher bar holds the water up, so the same stage then comes with less flow, and until hydrographers measure again the old curve reports too much water. They look for these shifts at every visit and correct the record, which is why the newest readings on a gauge page are marked provisional until someone has checked them.

A gauge page is best watched during a storm. When an atmospheric river, a long plume of moist air from the tropical Pacific (the Clouds course follows one in), is forecast, open the page for the Snoqualmie near Carnation and reload it a few times a day for three days. The National Weather Service posts river forecasts for many gauges, this one among them, but sketch your own first: when the peak will come, how high, and how fast the river will fall afterwards.

Water from rain that falls near the gauge reaches it within an hour or two. Rain on the far side of the basin, high on the North, Middle and South Forks of the Snoqualmie, which join near North Bend, has many miles of slope and channel to cross first. The river at the gauge is the sum of all of it, so it goes on rising long after the heaviest rain and peaks when the water from the far parts arrives. It falls more slowly than it rose, as the slopes go on draining for days. A city creek, with a small basin and much of it paved, rises and falls within hours.

blocks.caption: A model storm: the rain over the basin above, and below it the discharge at a gauge on a small city creek or a big river, drawn as the hours pass.
blocks.task: Guess when the big river peaks, then play the storm through for both

blocks.text: In the model the big river peaks about eleven hours after the heaviest rain and is still far above its starting flow a day later, while the creek peaks within two hours and has nearly settled by the next morning. Real rivers add more: snow that melts in a warm rain (lesson 2), and on some rivers a dam or a lake that holds back part of a flood, as the Masonry Dam does for the Cedar above the Renton gauge. A sketch made before the storm and set against the page afterwards shows which of these your river has.

blocks.caption: Six questions on measuring a creek
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why is an orange a good float for timing a creek's surface speed?
choices: It rides mostly under the surface, so it moves with the water and the wind barely pushes it
It is heavy enough to sink to mid-depth, so it moves at the average speed of the whole creek
It is large, so it averages the speed over a wide strip of the creek instead of one thin line
items.why: A float that sits high, like a leaf, is pushed by the breeze. An orange floats low and follows the surface water.

items.ask: Why multiply the orange's speed by about 0.8 to get the average speed down through the creek's depth?
choices: The bed slows the water touching it, so speed grows from near zero at the bed to its most at the top
The orange drifts from side to side as it floats, so it covers more than the 10 m it is timed over
The orange is pushed by the breeze as well as the water, so about a fifth of its speed is the wind's
items.why: Friction at the bed slows the bottom water, and each layer slows the one above. Over a gravel bed the average comes out near 0.8 of the surface speed.

items.ask: In a summer creek, why does the middle third of the width often carry far more than a third of the water?
choices: It is both the deepest part and the fastest, and a panel's flow is its area times its speed
It is where the orange floats, so the method counts the middle of a creek more than its edges
It is farther from both banks, so less of its water seeps into the gravel and is lost underground
items.why: Each panel's flow is its area times its speed. In the middle both are largest, so in the lesson's creek the middle third carried about two thirds of the water.

items.ask: A USGS gauge page gives a river's discharge every fifteen minutes. How is that number made?
choices: It measures the water's height and converts it with a curve fitted to flows measured by hand
It has a current meter fixed in the river that reads the speed at every depth and multiplies by width
It times floats released from a bridge, the same way you timed the orange in the creek
items.why: Gauges measure stage. Hydrographers visit every month or two to measure discharge directly, and the curve through those visits turns each stage into a discharge.

items.ask: A flood piles gravel on the bar just downstream of a gauge. Until hydrographers measure again, what does the page's discharge do?
choices: Reads too high: the raised bar holds the water up, so each stage now comes with less flow
Stays right: the gauge measures the water's height, which gives the flow whatever the bar is like
Reads too low: the raised bar narrows the channel, so the water speeds up and more flows at each stage
items.why: The bar holds the water back, so a higher bar raises the stage for the same flow. The old rating curve then gives too much water for each stage.

items.ask: Heavy rain falls at the same time over a big river's basin and over a small city creek's. Which describes their gauges best?
choices: The creek peaks within hours; the river many hours later, as water from far away arrives
Both peak in the hour of the heaviest rain, since the rain falls on each of them alike
The river peaks first, since its wide channel carries water faster than a narrow creek
items.why: Water from the far side of a big basin has many miles of slope and channel to cross, so the river keeps rising after the rain eases. A small, paved basin drains in hours.

sixtenths.title: Six-tenths of the way down
sixtenths.text: Hydrographers use the shape of the speed profile directly. In shallow water the speed six-tenths of the way down from the surface is close to the average for the whole depth, so they hold the current meter there. In deeper water they average two readings, at two-tenths and eight-tenths of the depth. The 0.8 rule for a float and the six-tenths rule for a meter come from the same profile.

cfs.title: Cubic feet a second
cfs.text: One cubic metre a second is 35.3 cfs. The Snoqualmie near Carnation runs at a few hundred cfs in a dry late summer and at tens of thousands in its biggest winter floods.

midsection.title: How many panels
midsection.text: USGS practice is to measure at twenty or more points across a stream, spaced so that no one panel carries much more than a twentieth of the flow. A mistake at a single point then cannot spoil the total.

well.title: The stilling well
well.text: The classic gauge is a vertical pipe or concrete well on the bank, joined to the river by pipes near the bottom. Ripples and waves cannot pass through the narrow pipes, so the water in the well rises and falls with the river but stays calm, and a float on it reads the stage to a hundredth of a foot.
